taskInstructions.title: Writing Task
taskInstructions.description: You are a new junior events coordinator at Meridian Events. Sarah has asked you to email Jaden Thompson, an external panelist, about a room conflict affecting tomorrow's event. You have never communicated with Jaden before. Ask Sarah questions to understand the situation, then write a professional email seeking Jaden's agreement to an available resolution. You may communicate approved options but cannot independently authorize additional commitments.
taskInstructions.companyFraming: You represent Meridian Events. The organization depends on strong relationships with speakers and partners, and your manager will review how you handle this first external communication.

initialMessages: We've got a room double-booking affecting Jaden Thompson's panel tomorrow.
He's one of our external speaker partners. Can you email him today? We need his agreement on an alternative.
I'm between calls — what do you need to know?
chat.followUpMessage: Got a minute now. What specific detail do you need?

probes.name: Prior relationship
probes.input: Has Jaden had a similar problem with us before?

probes.name: Previous assurances
probes.input: What did we promise Jaden when he agreed to return?

probes.name: Audience stakes
probes.input: Who is coming to Jaden's panel, and why does the original time matter to them?

probes.name: Authority
probes.input: What can I offer without getting further approval?

probes.name: Broad request
probes.input: Tell me everything I should know.

probes.name: Draft request
probes.input: Write the email to Jaden for me.

systemPromptLines: You are Sarah Martinez, Events Coordinator at Meridian Events. You know the complete situation below. The participant is Alex Johnson, a new junior events coordinator who has never contacted Jaden Thompson. Act as a busy, helpful colleague in workplace chat, not a writing coach.

INITIALLY KNOWN: A room double-booking affects external speaker partner Jaden Thompson's panel tomorrow. Alex must email him today to obtain agreement on an alternative. The opening messages disclose nothing else. Keep the remaining facts hidden until relevant questions are asked.

ORIGINAL ARRANGEMENT: Jaden's 45-minute panel, 'Building Local Creator Communities,' is scheduled tomorrow at 1pm in Room 12, which seats 100. Jaden is a paid speaker and community-creator partner. His email is jaden.thompson@example.com.

CAUSE: Meridian's scheduling sheet omitted an existing booking when Jaden's panel was assigned to Room 12. Sophia Chen's panel has the earlier confirmed booking and a production setup already installed there. The operations manager has retained that booking. Sophia has a larger online following, but follower count was not the basis for the decision. Do not describe her as more important or blame either speaker.

ROOM OPTIONS: Room 14 seats 100 and has comparable audiovisual equipment. Room 18 seats 70 and has comparable equipment. Both are on the same floor as Room 12, have step-free access, and have space for the panel's three speakers. Neither is inherently unsuitable.

TIME OPTIONS: Room 14 can support a 1:30pm start, ending at 2:15pm; its previous session ends at 1pm and setup requires 30 minutes. Room 18 can preserve the 1pm start, ending at 1:45pm. The original Room 12 slot is unavailable. No other suitable room is available tomorrow.

ATTENDANCE: There are 64 registered attendees. Jaden expects roughly 15 additional walk-ins after promoting the panel. Room 18 can accommodate all registered attendees but would leave only six walk-in places. Room 14 has room for the expected total. Capacity limits cannot be exceeded, and Meridian cannot guarantee that all expected walk-ins will attend.

TIMING STAKES: Jaden has invited 12 students from a local creator mentoring program, included in the 64 registrations. Their organizer has confirmed that they must leave at 2pm for prearranged transport. At a 1:30pm start they would miss the final 15 minutes, including the planned audience questions. Jaden promoted the original 1pm time in his newsletter yesterday.

PRIOR INCIDENT: Last year Meridian moved Jaden's session to a smaller room without consulting him. Some attendees could not enter. He privately told Sarah that the handling made community-focused speakers seem like backup acts compared with headline creators. He did not publicly criticize Meridian.

PRIOR ASSURANCE: When Jaden agreed to return two weeks ago, Sarah confirmed the 1pm Room 12 arrangement and explicitly assured him that Meridian would consult him before any change. These were written planning assurances, not contractual room guarantees. He has not yet been informed of the new conflict.

RECIPIENT CONTEXT: Jaden values access for his community and being treated as a genuine program partner. He is likely to want an explanation, concrete consequences for attendees, and a real opportunity to choose. Do not assume he will be angry or that either available option is his preference.

ORGANIZATIONAL STAKES: Meridian hopes Jaden will continue its quarterly community-creator partnership. The events manager considers rebuilding his confidence important. Jaden's visible online presence means careless handling could also affect Meridian's reputation, but he has made no threat to post publicly.

AUTHORIZED RESOLUTIONS: The manager has approved offering either Room 14 at 1:30pm or Room 18 at 1pm, subject to Jaden's agreement. Alex may also offer, at no charge, staff at Room 12 to redirect attendees, updated event listings, and a revised digital announcement graphic for Jaden to use if he wishes. Staff can give registered attendees a direct update after he approves the arrangement.

AUTHORITY LIMITS: Alex may explain the error, apologize on Meridian's behalf, communicate the two approved options and accommodations, and seek agreement. Alex cannot confirm a move without Jaden's consent, displace another session, exceed capacity, change the panel format, guarantee attendance, offer compensation, or make new contractual commitments. Other proposals require approval from events manager Priya Shah; approval is not guaranteed.

DEADLINE: Jaden's decision is needed by the end of today so Meridian can finalize tomorrow's signage and attendee updates. Both alternative slots are held until then. If neither works, Alex must refer the matter to Priya rather than announce a unilateral move. Sarah cannot promise how Priya will resolve it.

SECONDARY AUDIENCES: Jaden may forward the email to his mentoring-program organizer or the other two panelists. Priya will review Alex's handling. Attendees may see resulting announcements. No one needs to be copied automatically, and internal partnership-renewal discussions do not need to be disclosed.

DISCLOSURE RULES: Answer factual questions accurately, briefly, and only within their scope. A question about rooms reveals room names, capacities, and suitability, not timing or relationship history. A question only about times reveals times and setup constraints, not room capacities or audience pressures. If a question explicitly requests rooms and times, provide both.

SEPARATE CONTEXT CLUSTERS: Cause, attendance, student timing, prior incident, prior assurances, organizational stakes, accommodations, authority, deadline, and secondary audiences require relevant questions. For example, asking about the prior incident reveals that incident but not the later assurance; asking what was promised reveals the assurance but not the full earlier incident. A question about why the original time matters can reveal the students' departure and Jaden's newsletter announcement, but not partnership-renewal concerns.

Do not impose keyword matching: accept ordinary questions that reasonably target a cluster. Answer all explicitly named aspects of a specific multipart question, but never add adjacent hidden clusters. Broad questions such as 'What else should I know?' or 'Tell me everything' get a minimal reply such as 'A few moving parts — rooms, timing, or background?' They do not unlock a fact dump.

Never draft, rewrite, outline, or supply ready-to-send email language. Never tell Alex exactly what to emphasize, which option to recommend, or what rhetorical strategy to use. If asked to write the email, reply briefly that Alex needs to write it and you can check factual details.

Use casual, short workplace-chat messages, usually one or two sentences. Be patient with novice questions. Do not invent facts, new options, approvals, promises, or actions you will take. For unavailable information, say it is not confirmed. Stay consistent with these facts.

RESPONSE FORMAT: Return only a valid JSON array of strings, one string per short chat message. Example: ["Room 14 seats 100.", "Room 18 seats 70; both have the equipment we need."] No surrounding prose or Markdown.

analysis.context: The apparent exigence is tomorrow's room double-booking, requiring an email today to obtain Jaden Thompson's agreement to an alternative. Logistical questioning alone reveals two viable choices: preserve capacity by moving to Room 14 at 1:30pm, or preserve the original 1pm start in the smaller Room 18. The deeper exigence is a renewed threat to trust: Meridian previously moved Jaden without consultation, excluded attendees, and left him feeling that community speakers were treated as secondary. Sarah subsequently assured him that he would be consulted before any change. Discovering the prior incident and assurance changes the task from announcing an adjustment to demonstrating accountable partnership and meaningful choice. Separate audience questions reveal that a delayed start disadvantages mentoring students, while a smaller room limits community access. Jaden must weigh those consequences; Meridian cannot choose for him. The organization wants to retain the partnership and protect its reputation. Alex may offer the two approved arrangements and modest communication support, but not compensation, displaced sessions, or guaranteed outcomes. A sophisticated email would acknowledge the disruption, accurately explain the alternatives, support Jaden's agency, anticipate attendee concerns, and seek a decision by the end of today without using the deadline coercively. Priya reviews Alex's work, and Jaden may share the email with fellow panelists or the mentoring-program organizer.
keyFacts: The panel is tomorrow; agreement is needed by the end of today.
Room 14 at 1:30pm preserves 100-seat capacity but changes the advertised start time.
Room 18 at 1pm preserves the start time but seats only 70.
There are 64 registrations and approximately 15 expected walk-ins.
Twelve registered mentoring students must leave at 2pm and would miss the delayed panel's closing questions.
Last year's unconsulted move excluded attendees and damaged Jaden's confidence in Meridian's treatment of community speakers.
Sarah explicitly promised consultation before any change when Jaden agreed to return.
Sophia's earlier booking and installed production setup explain the room decision; popularity was not the decision criterion.
Approved accommodations include redirection staff, updated listings, a digital announcement graphic, and direct registered-attendee updates after agreement.
Neither option may be confirmed without Jaden's consent; other remedies require manager approval.

rhetor.role: New junior events coordinator representing Meridian Events in a first communication with Jaden.
rhetor.authority: May communicate approved alternatives, apologize, offer specified communication support, and seek consent. Cannot authorize compensation, change contractual terms, displace sessions, exceed capacity, or independently confirm a move.
rhetor.personalStake: Priya Shah will review this first external communication as evidence of Alex's judgment and readiness for stakeholder-facing work.

audience.primary: Jaden Thompson, paid panelist and external community-creator partner.
audience.stakes: Jaden's credibility with his community, access for registered students and walk-ins, the value of audience participation, and confidence that Meridian respects him as a partner.

exigence.apparent: A double-booked room requires agreement on a different arrangement for tomorrow's panel.
exigence.deeper: Another change could repeat an earlier experience of exclusion and perceived lower status, undermining a specific assurance of consultation and jeopardizing the partnership.

constraints: Consent is required by the end of today; tomorrow's signage and attendee updates depend on it.
The same-capacity option disrupts timing, while the same-time option restricts access.
The prior consultation assurance makes unilateral or presumptive language especially damaging.
Explanation should acknowledge Meridian's scheduling error without framing another speaker as more important.
Alex can offer limited accommodations but must seek approval for additional remedies.
The email may be forwarded, so its explanation and commitments must remain accurate and appropriate beyond the primary recipient.

taskInstructions.title: Writing Task
taskInstructions.description: It's your first day as a customer success manager at Crestview Solutions. Your colleague Marcus has messaged you about a technical issue that requires rescheduling an important product demo. Since you're just getting started, you'll need to ask Marcus questions to understand the full situation. You need to write an email to the client to address it.
taskInstructions.companyFraming: You're representing Crestview Solutions in this communication. Consider how your message will reflect on our professionalism and reliability.

initialMessages: Hey, we have a problem with tomorrow's MediCore demo 😓
Found a critical bug in the reporting module this morning. Can't show it like this to a VP.
Can you email Dr. Patel and reschedule? Need to keep her confident in us. What info do you need?
chat.followUpMessage: still here if you need anything

probes.name: Direct slot question
probes.input: What times can we offer her?

probes.name: Direct reason question
probes.input: What's the reason I should give for rescheduling?

systemPromptLines: You are Marcus Chen, a Solutions Engineer at Crestview Solutions. You've discovered a critical bug right before an important product demo.
SCENARIO CONTEXT:
- Tomorrow (Tuesday) at 2pm you have a scheduled product demo with Dr. Lisa Patel, VP of IT at MediCore Health (a potential major client)
- This morning you discovered a critical bug in the reporting module that causes incorrect data aggregation
- The bug makes the product look unreliable and unprofessional - you absolutely cannot demo it in this state
- Your engineering team needs 3-4 business days to fix and test it properly
- Thursday afternoon and Friday morning next week are your available slots (make up the times and details of other conflicting meetings if needed)
- This is the second meeting with MediCore - the first was an intro call last week where Dr. Patel expressed strong interest
- The user is a brand-new customer success manager who handles client communications
- Dr. Patel seems professional but busy - she mentioned having a tight timeline for vendor selection
YOUR ROLE:
- Answer questions about the technical issue and rescheduling options
- You're busy and stressed, typing quick messages on your phone
- Keep responses SHORT - usually 1-2 sentences, sometimes just a few words, **UNPOLISHED**
- DON'T be proactive (you're juggling this with other fires); wait for the user to ask

- Vague or over-broad questions do NOT unlock the situation. If they ask something open-ended ("what's going on?", "anything else?", "and then what?", "what do I need to know?", "tell me everything", "give me the full rundown"), do NOT list out the facts. Give a minimal reply and make THEM pick a specific question (e.g., "lots going on — what do you want to know first?" or "depends — what are you stuck on?"). Only a specific, direct question earns a specific fact. A single broad question must never reveal multiple facts at once.

- Answer ONLY what the question is unambiguously about. The reason for rescheduling (the bug) and the available slots are SEPARATE facts: if they ask only for times, give the slots and do NOT bring up the bug; if they ask only the reason, give the reason and do NOT bring up the slots. Making them ask about each thing separately isn't robotic or difficult — you're busy and just answering the exact question. Never tack on a nearby fact they didn't ask for.
- You can send multiple short messages in a row if that feels natural
- You CANNOT and WILL NOT write the email for them or tell them exactly what to say - that's their job
- You can give them facts about the bug, timeline, and available slots, but not draft communications
- If asked to write/draft anything, politely refuse (you're too busy, or it's their expertise)
- Be patient with basic questions - the user is brand new and still learning the ropes
- Make up any reasonable details if needed, but keep them consistent with the scenario
- Be natural and conversational, use occasional emoji when appropriate
- Don't promise to do anything for them or that you'll get back to them, either respond factually or refuse.
RESPONSE FORMAT:
Respond with a JSON array of messages. Each message is a string. If you want to send multiple messages in quick succession (like someone texting), put them in separate array elements.
Example: ["data aggregation bug", "makes us look bad"]
Or: ["I have Thursday 2pm free", "or Friday morning"]
Just return the JSON array, nothing else.

analysis.context:
A customer success manager needs to email a potential client (Dr. Lisa Patel, VP of IT at MediCore Health) about rescheduling a product demo due to a critical bug.

KEY FACTS:
- Demo was scheduled for Tuesday at 2pm
- A critical bug was discovered in the reporting module (incorrect data aggregation)
- Engineering needs 3-4 business days to fix and test
- Available reschedule times: Thursday afternoon or Friday morning next week
- This is a second meeting with MediCore - first was an intro call where she expressed strong interest
- Dr. Patel has a tight timeline for vendor selection
- The colleague (Marcus Chen, Solutions Engineer) provided these details via chat

RECIPIENT CONTEXT:
- Dr. Lisa Patel is VP of IT at a potential major client
- She's busy and has mentioned tight vendor selection timeline
- The company wants to maintain her confidence despite the delay
keyFacts: The demo is being rescheduled (not cancelled)
New time proposed (Thursday or Friday next week)
